content: Staphylococcus aureus, often referred to as golden staph, is a spherical bacterium that is a common cause of staph infections. It is frequently found on the skin or in the nasal passages of humans, with approximately 20–30% of the population being carriers. This bacterium can cause a wide spectrum of illnesses, ranging from minor skin infections, such as pimples, impetigo, boils, cellulitis, folliculitis, furuncles, carbuncles, scalded skin syndrome, and abscesses, to severe and life-threatening conditions, including pneumonia, meningitis, osteomyelitis, endocarditis, toxic shock syndrome (TSS), and septicemia. It is associated with infections of the skin, soft tissues, respiratory system, bones, joints, endovascular structures, and wounds. Staphylococcus aureus remains one of the leading causes of nosocomial (hospital-acquired) infections, particularly post-surgical wound infections. In microbiology, Staphylococcus aureus is a Gram-positive coccus that appears as grape-like clusters under a microscope. When cultured on blood agar plates, it forms large, round, golden-yellow colonies, often exhibiting hemolysis. The golden pigmentation is the origin of its name, as aureus means golden in Latin. It is a facultative anaerobe and an opportunistic pathogen. Staphylococcus aureus is catalase-positive, meaning it produces the enzyme catalase, which converts hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. This property helps distinguish it from other bacteria like streptococci and enterococci. Additionally, most strains of Staphylococcus aureus are coagulase-positive, producing the enzyme coagulase, which facilitates clot formation. However, some atypical strains may not produce coagulase, which can complicate identification and impact treatment decisions. Staphylococcus aureus is known for its aggressive nature and its potential for antibiotic resistance. Staphylococcus aureus can exist as a commensal organism on human skin, in the nasal passages, and occasionally in the throat. Its presence in these areas does not always indicate infection and may not require treatment, as re-colonization is common. It can also survive on domesticated animals, such as dogs, cats, and horses, and is known to cause bumblefoot in chickens. The bacterium can persist on dry environmental surfaces for hours, although the role of environmental surfaces in its transmission remains debated. Staphylococcus aureus can harbor bacteriophages, such as the Panton-Valentine leukocidin (PVL), which enhance its virulence. The bacterium can invade the skin or mucosal linings, leading to localized infections like furuncles (boils) and carbuncles (clusters of boils). In infants, it can cause a severe condition known as staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS). Transmission occurs through contact with pus from infected wounds, direct skin-to-skin contact with an infected individual, or contact with contaminated objects like towels, sheets, clothing, or athletic equipment. Deep-seated infections caused by Staphylococcus aureus can be particularly severe, especially in individuals with prosthetic joints, which increase the risk of septic arthritis, staphylococcal endocarditis (infection of the heart valves), and rapidly spreading pneumonia. In patients with atopic dermatitis, Staphylococcus aureus is highly prevalent and often causes complications. These patients are more susceptible to the bacterium than the general population. The infection is commonly found in areas with active sebaceous glands, such as the armpits, scalp, and hair-bearing regions. Large pimples in these areas, when ruptured, can exacerbate the infection. Certain strains of Staphylococcus aureus produce toxins that cause toxic shock syndrome (TSS). These strains secrete toxic shock syndrome toxin (TSST-1), which is the primary cause of TSS, particularly in association with tampon use. Other strains produce enterotoxins, which are responsible for staphylococcal food poisoning. Staphylococcus aureus is also a causative agent of mastitis in dairy cows, where its large capsule protects it from the cow's immune defenses. Staphylococcus aureus produces a variety of toxins that contribute to its virulence. These toxins can be categorized into three groups, many of which are associated with specific diseases. Pyrogenic toxin superantigens (PTSAgs), such as TSST-1, induce toxic shock syndrome. Staphylococcal enterotoxins, which cause food poisoning, are also part of this group. Exfoliative toxins are implicated in staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS), a condition most commonly seen in infants and young children, and occasionally in hospital nursery outbreaks. The protease activity of these toxins causes the characteristic skin peeling observed in SSSS. Other toxins, such as alpha-toxin, beta-toxin, delta-toxin, and bicomponent toxins like Panton-Valentine leukocidin (PVL), act on cell membranes. PVL is associated with severe necrotizing pneumonia in children and is encoded by genes found on bacteriophages in community-associated MRSA strains. The vivid yellow pigmentation of Staphylococcus aureus may play a role in its virulence. Studies comparing pigmented and non-pigmented strains have shown that the yellow-pigmented strains are more resistant to oxidative stress, such as exposure to hydrogen peroxide, and are better able to survive attacks by human neutrophils. In animal models, wounds infected with pigmented strains resulted in persistent abscesses, whereas wounds infected with non-pigmented strains healed more quickly. These findings suggest that the yellow pigment, which is due to carotenoid production, may enhance the bacterium's ability to evade the immune system. Drugs that inhibit carotenoid production could potentially weaken the bacterium and restore its susceptibility to antibiotics.
